topic: What testing is and why it matters

notes.front: What is testing?
notes.back: The process within the software development lifecycle that evaluates the quality of a component or system and related work products.
notes.explanation: The definition names related work products as well as the component or system, so testing is not limited to running code.
notes.example: Like a building inspector who checks the architect’s drawings as well as the finished walls.
notes.evidence: The process within the software development lifecycle that evaluates the quality of a component or system and related work products.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “testing”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test object?
notes.back: The work product that is being tested.
notes.explanation: The syllabus uses the name for software work products while they are under test, so the same item is a test object only for as long as it is being tested.
notes.example: Like whichever car is on the inspection ramp: it is “the car under test” until it drives off.
notes.evidence: The work product to be tested.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test object”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is verification?
notes.back: Confirming that a work product fulfils its specification.
notes.explanation: The yardstick is the written specification, so verification asks whether the product was built as specified.
notes.example: Like checking a flat-pack wardrobe against its assembly drawing, panel by panel.
notes.evidence: The process of confirming that a work product fulfills its specification.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “verification”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is validation?
notes.back: Confirmation, by examination, that a work product matches a stakeholder’s needs.
notes.explanation: The yardstick is what stakeholders need, which is not necessarily what a specification says.
notes.example: Like asking the family who ordered the wardrobe whether it actually holds their coats and fits the alcove.
notes.evidence: Confirmation by examination that a work product matches a
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “validation”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a test objective?
notes.back: The purpose for testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists nine typical objectives and says the ones that apply vary with the context.
notes.example: Like the purpose of a medical check-up, which might be to rule out one illness or to confirm fitness for a marathon.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “test objective”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1, pp. 15–16
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is debugging?
notes.back: The process of finding, analysing and removing the causes of failures in a component or system.
notes.explanation: It starts from failures and works back to their causes; the syllabus treats it as an activity separate from testing.
notes.example: Like a mechanic tracing the rattle a driver reported to a loose bolt and tightening it.
notes.evidence: The process of finding, analyzing and removing the causes of failures in a component or system.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “debugging”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is quality?
notes.back: The degree to which a work product satisfies stated and implied requirements.
notes.explanation: Implied requirements count as well as stated ones, so meeting every written requirement is not the whole of quality.
notes.example: Like a hotel room: no booking says “the shower runs hot”, yet guests judge the room by it.
notes.evidence: The degree to which a work product satisfies stated and implied requirements.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “quality”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is quality assurance (QA)?
notes.back: Activities focused on providing confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled.
notes.explanation: It is about confidence that requirements will be met; the syllabus adds that it works on processes and aims to prevent problems.
notes.example: Like a restaurant’s hygiene routines, which aim to make every meal safe, rather than tasting one finished dish.
notes.evidence: Activities focused on providing confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “quality assurance”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is an error?
notes.back: A human action that results in a defect.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also calls errors mistakes. An error is something a person does, not something in the product.
notes.example: Like a typist hitting the wrong key: the slip is the error, the wrong letter on the page is what it leaves behind.
notes.evidence: A human action that results in a defect.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “error”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a defect?
notes.back: An imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications, or impairs its intended use.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also calls defects faults or bugs. A defect sits in a work product, whether or not anyone has run into it yet.
notes.example: Like a hairline crack in a window pane, which is there even on calm days.
notes.evidence: An imperfection or deficiency in a work product where it does not meet its requirements or specifications or impairs its intended use.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “defect”; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a failure?
notes.back: An event in which a component or system does not meet its requirements within specified limits during its execution.
notes.explanation: A failure is an event during execution, so it is something that happens, not something that sits in a document.
notes.example: Like the moment the cracked pane actually gives way in a storm.
notes.evidence: An event in which a component or system does not meet its requirements within specified limits during its execution.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “failure”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is a root cause?
notes.back: A source of a defect such that removing it reduces or removes the occurrence of that type of defect.
notes.explanation: The definition speaks of a defect type, so dealing with a root cause affects future defects of that kind, not only the one in hand.
notes.example: Like finding that one supplier’s faulty batch of glass lies behind many cracked panes.
notes.evidence: A source of a defect such that if it is removed, the occurrence of the defect type is decreased or removed.
notes.source: ISTQB Glossary, “root cause”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0

notes.front: What is root cause analysis?
notes.back: The analysis that identifies root causes, typically carried out when a failure occurs or a defect is identified.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says addressing a root cause is believed to prevent similar failures or defects, or to reduce how often they happen.
notes.example: Like a railway investigating why signals keep failing along a whole line, rather than just resetting one signal.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, what cognitive level of knowledge is K1?
notes.back: Remember: recognising, remembering or recalling a keyword or concept.
notes.explanation: The syllabus says, in general, all the content of chapters 1 to 6 is examinable at this level, and keywords listed under chapter headings shall be remembered.
notes.example: Like knowing that a failure is an event during execution, without yet being asked to use the idea.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 0.5 “Examinable Learning Objectives and Cognitive Level of Knowledge”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, what cognitive level of knowledge is K2?
notes.back: Understand.
notes.explanation: Learning objectives at this level use verbs such as explain, differentiate and exemplify, which ask for more than recall.
notes.example: Like being able to explain how a failure differs from a defect, not just recite both definitions.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 0.5 “Examinable Learning Objectives and Cognitive Level of Knowledge”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the syllabus, what cognitive level of knowledge is K3?
notes.back: Apply.
notes.explanation: It is the highest of the three levels the syllabus uses for its learning objectives.
notes.example: Like using a technique on a new problem, rather than explaining how the technique works.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 0.5 “Examinable Learning Objectives and Cognitive Level of Knowledge”, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the exam rules as changed on 2 May 2025, at what level are syllabus keywords examinable?
notes.back: K2: for understanding their definition.
notes.explanation: The syllabus itself says keywords shall be remembered (K1); the later exam rule raises the bar to understanding.
notes.source: ISTQB Exam Structures and Rules v1.2, rule 4.1.4, p. 8; CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 0.5, p. 11
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the first common misconception about testing that the syllabus corrects?
notes.back: That testing consists only of executing tests: running the software and checking the results.
notes.explanation: Testing also covers work such as planning, analysis and reviews, and it has to fit in with the development lifecycle.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the second common misconception about testing that the syllabus corrects?
notes.back: That testing focuses entirely on verifying the test object.
notes.explanation: Testing also validates: it asks whether the system serves the people who will use it, in the setting where they will use it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What separates dynamic testing from static testing?
notes.back: Dynamic testing executes the software; static testing does not.
notes.explanation: Static testing includes reviews and static analysis, while dynamic testing derives test cases with test techniques and approaches.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides being a technical activity, what else does testing need?
notes.back: Proper management: planning, estimating, monitoring and controlling.
notes.explanation: The syllabus stresses that testing is not only technical, and returns to its management in chapter 5.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Testers use tools, but what kind of activity does the syllabus say testing largely is?
notes.back: An intellectual activity.
notes.explanation: It asks testers for specialised knowledge, analytical skills, critical thinking and systems thinking.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A project manager proposes to “save time” by skipping everything in testing except running the automated suite the night before release. Which misconception is this?
notes.back: A: that testing only consists of executing tests.
notes.choices:
A) That testing only consists of executing tests
B) That testing focuses entirely on verification
C) That exhaustive testing is possible
notes.choicesExplained: B would be about ignoring stakeholders’ needs, which the proposal does not mention. C concerns testing everything, not skipping activities.
notes.explanation: Running tests is one activity among several; the rest of testing, such as planning and reviews, is what the proposal drops.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between verification and validation?
notes.back: Verification checks the system against its specified requirements; validation checks whether it meets the needs of users and other stakeholders where it will be used.
notes.explanation: A product can match its specification perfectly and still not suit the people who use it, which is why testing needs both.
notes.contrast: Verification: built as specified? Validation: right for the people who will use it?
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester compares each field of a new invoice screen with the approved specification. Is this verification or validation?
notes.back: Verification.
notes.explanation: The yardstick here is the specification, not what the people using the screen need.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Farm workers try a new harvest-logging app in the field and find they cannot use the tiny buttons in gloves, though every specified requirement passes. Is this verification or validation?
notes.back: Validation.
notes.explanation: The check is against users’ needs in the real operating environment, which the specification failed to capture.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1 “What is Testing?”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective targets requirements, user stories, designs and code as items to be evaluated?
notes.back: Evaluating work products.
notes.explanation: Static testing, such as reviews, does this without running any code.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective is about provoking the software to misbehave and tracking down what is wrong?
notes.back: Causing failures and finding defects.
notes.explanation: Failures reveal defects; finding them is how testing supports later removal by debugging.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective is about exercising enough of the test object?
notes.back: Ensuring the required coverage of the test object.
notes.explanation: The aim is that the tests exercise as much of the test object as was required; chapter 4 shows how coverage is measured for each technique.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective concerns the chance that the software turns out not good enough?
notes.back: Reducing the risk level of inadequate software quality.
notes.explanation: Testing can lower this risk but not remove it, because finding no defects does not prove that none remain.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective checks the product against its specified requirements?
notes.back: Verifying whether the specified requirements have been fulfilled.
notes.explanation: This is verification in its plain sense: the specification is the yardstick.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective is about contracts, laws and regulators?
notes.back: Verifying that the test object complies with contractual, legal and regulatory requirements.
notes.explanation: Some requirements come from outside the project, and testing can show they are met.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective serves people who have to make decisions about the product?
notes.back: Providing information to stakeholders so they can make informed decisions.
notes.explanation: Test results are evidence; decisions such as whether to release depend on them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective concerns how sure people can be about the test object’s quality?
notes.back: Building confidence in the quality of the test object.
notes.explanation: Passing tests give grounds for confidence, though not proof of correctness.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which typical test objective uses stakeholders’ expectations, rather than the specification, as the yardstick?
notes.back: Validating whether the test object is complete and works as the stakeholders expect.
notes.explanation: It is the validation counterpart of verifying specified requirements.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Before a regulator’s visit, a pharmacy chain tests its new prescription system to show it keeps records exactly as the law requires. Which test objective is uppermost?
notes.back: B: verifying compliance with legal and regulatory requirements.
notes.choices:
A) Causing failures and finding defects
B) Verifying compliance with contractual, legal and regulatory requirements
C) Ensuring required coverage
notes.choicesExplained: A is a by-product, not the aim here. C is about how much is exercised, not what the law demands.
notes.explanation: The driver is an external legal obligation, which is exactly what the compliance objective covers.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A product owner asks the testers for a summary of open problems so she can decide whether Friday’s launch goes ahead. Which test objective does the summary serve?
notes.back: A: providing information for informed decisions.
notes.choices:
A) Providing information to stakeholders for informed decisions
B) Evaluating work products
C) Validating that the test object works as stakeholders expect
notes.choicesExplained: B is about examining items such as requirements or code. C would be checking the product against expectations, not reporting for a decision.
notes.explanation: The testing output here feeds a go or no-go decision, which is what this objective is for.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 15
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What makes test objectives vary from one project to another?
notes.back: The context, for example the work product tested, the test level and the risks.
notes.explanation: The syllabus also names the lifecycle being followed and business factors such as corporate structure, competition and time to market.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.1 “Test Objectives”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does testing differ from debugging?
notes.back: Testing triggers failures or finds defects; debugging finds, analyses and removes their causes.
notes.explanation: The syllabus calls them separate activities: one exposes problems, the other deals with them.
notes.contrast: Testing exposes the problem; debugging removes its cause.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After dynamic testing triggers a failure, what is the first step of the typical debugging process?
notes.back: Reproducing the failure.
notes.explanation: Reproduction comes before diagnosis and fixing in the typical process.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the typical debugging process, what does the diagnosis step do?
notes.back: It finds the defect behind the failure.
notes.explanation: Diagnosis sits between reproducing the failure and fixing the defect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the last step of the typical debugging process after a failure?
notes.back: Fixing the defect.
notes.explanation: Once diagnosis has located the defect, it can be removed; later testing then checks the fix.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After debugging, what kind of testing checks whether the fix actually solved the problem?
notes.back: Confirmation testing.
notes.explanation: It follows debugging and is itself testing, not part of debugging.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Who should preferably carry out the confirmation testing after a fix?
notes.back: The same person who carried out the original test.
notes.explanation: The syllabus states this as a preference, not a strict rule.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What may follow confirmation testing, and what does it look for?
notes.back: Regression testing, which checks that the fixes have not broken anything elsewhere in the test object.
notes.explanation: A fix can have side effects elsewhere, and regression testing is the check for them.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When static testing finds a defect, which debugging steps are not needed?
notes.back: Reproduction and diagnosis: debugging only has to remove the defect.
notes.explanation: A static defect is found directly, with no failure behind it, because static testing never runs the code; there is nothing to reproduce or trace.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In a review, a tester spots that a pricing specification gives the wrong discount rate. What does debugging involve here?
notes.back: B: simply removing the defect by correcting the rate.
notes.choices:
A) Reproducing the failure, diagnosing it, then fixing the defect
B) Simply correcting the rate in the specification
C) Nothing: reviews do not lead to debugging
notes.choicesExplained: A applies when dynamic testing triggers a failure; here nothing was run. C is wrong: a defect found statically still has to be removed.
notes.explanation: A review is static testing, which points straight at the defect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tester makes the checkout crash with a long voucher code. A developer then makes it crash again on her machine, traces it to an unchecked string length and patches it. Which part was testing?
notes.back: A: only the tester triggering the crash.
notes.choices:
A) Only the tester triggering the crash
B) Everything the developer did
C) All of it
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: reproducing, tracing and patching are the steps of debugging, which the syllabus keeps separate from testing.
notes.explanation: Testing triggered the failure; the developer’s reproduction, diagnosis and fix make up debugging.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.1.2 “Testing and Debugging”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: As a form of what does the syllabus describe testing?
notes.back: Quality control.
notes.explanation: As quality control, testing helps the project reach its agreed test objectives while staying within its scope, schedule, quality and budget limits.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2 “Why is Testing Necessary?”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Running tests on a finished release candidate to find its defects: quality control or quality assurance?
notes.back: Quality control: testing is a major form of it.
notes.explanation: Testing is product-oriented and corrective, and it is a major form of quality control; QA would change the process rather than examine this release.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contribution of testing raises test-object quality only indirectly?
notes.back: Detecting defects cost-effectively, so that debugging can remove them.
notes.explanation: Testing itself removes nothing: debugging, a non-testing activity, does the removal.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contribution of testing feeds decisions such as moving to the next lifecycle phase or releasing?
notes.back: Directly evaluating the test object’s quality at various phases.
notes.explanation: These measures form part of wider project management.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contribution of testing stands in for users on the development project?
notes.back: Giving users indirect representation: testers make sure their understanding of users’ needs is considered.
notes.explanation: Bringing a truly representative group of real users into the project is rarely practical: it costs too much, and suitable users are hard to find.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which contribution of testing comes from contracts, the law or regulators?
notes.back: Meeting contractual or legal requirements, or complying with regulatory standards.
notes.explanation: In some settings testing is required, not optional.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Test results show 3 open minor problems and none serious; the steering group uses this to approve moving to the beta phase. Which contribution of testing is at work?
notes.back: A: directly evaluating quality to support a phase decision.
notes.choices:
A) Directly evaluating quality at a lifecycle phase
B) Indirect representation of users
C) Meeting regulatory standards
notes.choicesExplained: B is about considering users’ needs throughout development. C involves a legal or regulatory duty, which is not mentioned.
notes.explanation: The measures feed a decision to move to the next phase, as the syllabus describes.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A tax-return app cannot bring thousands of taxpayers into the team, so testers work through scenarios the way a first-time filer would. Which contribution is this?
notes.back: B: giving users indirect representation.
notes.choices:
A) Detecting defects cost-effectively
B) Indirect representation of users
C) Direct evaluation for the release decision
notes.choicesExplained: A and C may also happen, but the point of the scenarios is to bring users’ needs into development.
notes.explanation: Testers stand in for users because involving a representative set of them is usually impractical.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.1 “Testing’s Contributions to Success”, p. 16
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Are testing and quality assurance the same thing?
notes.back: No, although people often use the two terms interchangeably.
notes.explanation: They differ in focus and aim: one works on the product, the other on the processes.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does testing differ from QA in orientation and approach?
notes.back: Testing is product-oriented and corrective; QA is process-oriented and preventive.
notes.explanation: Testing looks at a product to correct it; QA improves the way work is done so problems do not arise.
notes.contrast: Testing: product, corrective. QA: process, preventive.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On what assumption does QA work?
notes.back: That a good process, followed correctly, will produce a good product.
notes.explanation: This is why QA spends its effort on implementing and improving processes.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which processes does QA apply to, and who is responsible for it?
notes.back: Both development and testing processes; everyone on the project is responsible.
notes.explanation: Responsibility is shared across the whole project, and QA looks after the testing processes as well as the development ones.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which form of quality control other than testing includes model checking and proof of correctness?
notes.back: Formal methods.
notes.explanation: Testing is a major form of quality control, but not the only one.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides testing and formal methods, which two forms of quality control does the syllabus name?
notes.back: Simulation and prototyping.
notes.explanation: Testing is a major form of quality control, but it shares that role with these and with formal methods.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does testing use test results?
notes.back: To get defects fixed.
notes.explanation: QA uses the same results differently, as feedback on processes.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does QA use test results?
notes.back: As feedback on how well the development and test processes are performing.
notes.explanation: QA is process-oriented, so results tell it about the processes rather than one product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A company makes a design checklist mandatory for every change, to improve how its teams build software. Is this testing or QA?
notes.back: QA.
notes.explanation: It changes a process to prevent problems, rather than examining one product to correct it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Defect counts show that most bugs in the last 3 releases came from rushed code reviews, and the team changes its review process. Whose use of test results is this?
notes.back: QA: the results are feedback on how the process performs.
notes.explanation: Testing would use the same results to get the individual defects fixed.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.2 “Testing and Quality Assurance (QA)”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In v4.0.1, what did the syllabus’s section on QA start comparing QA with?
notes.back: Testing: the errata replaced the words “quality control” with “testing” there.
notes.explanation: The release notes explain that the section compares QA with testing, not with quality control.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, Appendix C “Release Notes”, “Corrections in the text”, p. 73
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What other names does the syllabus give errors and defects?
notes.back: Errors are also mistakes; defects are also faults or bugs.
notes.explanation: The glossary likewise lists mistake as a synonym of error, and bug and fault among the synonyms of defect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Humans make errors, which produce defects, which in turn {{c1::may}} result in failures.
notes.explanation: The hedge matters: a defect does not always lead to a failure.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which reason for human errors does a tight deadline illustrate?
notes.back: Time pressure.
notes.explanation: The syllabus lists it first among several reasons people make errors.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What property of work products, processes, infrastructure or interactions can lead people into errors?
notes.back: Their complexity.
notes.explanation: The more intricate the work, the more room there is for human slips.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two personal reasons for errors does the syllabus give?
notes.back: Being tired, and lacking adequate training.
notes.explanation: Errors come from people, so the state and preparation of the person matter.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A user guide gives the wrong keyboard shortcut for saving a file. In which kind of place is this defect?
notes.back: Documentation.
notes.explanation: Defects can sit in documents such as guides, specifications and test scripts, not only in code.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A wrong database address in the deployment configuration stops every test environment from starting. Where does the defect sit?
notes.back: In a supporting work product: the deployment configuration.
notes.explanation: The configuration is neither documentation nor source code, but it supports the product, so it is a supporting work product like a build file.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What often happens to a defect in an early work product that nobody detects?
notes.back: It often leads to defective work products later in the lifecycle.
notes.explanation: Later work is built from earlier work, so an early defect is copied forward.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When defective code is executed, what are the two ways the system can fail?
notes.back: It may leave out something it is supposed to do, or do something it is not supposed to do.
notes.explanation: Both count as failures: a missing behaviour and an unwanted one.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does every defect cause a failure when it is executed?
notes.back: No. Some always do, some only in specific circumstances, and some may never cause one.
notes.explanation: Whether a defect shows up can depend on the circumstances in which the code runs.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A defect in a booking system only makes it misbehave on 29 February. Which kind of defect is this?
notes.back: One that results in a failure only in specific circumstances.
notes.explanation: The defect is executed every day, but it only produces a failure when the particular date comes round.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Besides errors and defects, what else can cause failures?
notes.back: Environmental conditions.
notes.explanation: So a failure does not always trace back to a human error and a defect in the work product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A roadside ticket machine starts misbehaving only in heatwaves, when its casing overheats; nobody has changed its software. What kind of cause should the team consider?
notes.back: An environmental condition.
notes.explanation: Failures can come from the physical environment, not only from errors and defects.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer, rushed before a public holiday, misreads the rule and sets the child-fare age limit to 12 instead of 16. A 14-year-old is then charged the adult fare. What is the rush before the holiday, in this chain?
notes.back: A likely root cause: the situation that led to the error.
notes.explanation: A root cause is a fundamental reason for a problem, such as a situation that leads to an error.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer, rushed before a public holiday, misreads the rule and sets the child-fare age limit to 12 instead of 16. A 14-year-old is then charged the adult fare. What is the developer’s misreading, in this chain?
notes.back: The error (mistake).
notes.explanation: It is the human action that results in the defect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer, rushed before a public holiday, misreads the rule and sets the child-fare age limit to 12 instead of 16. A 14-year-old is then charged the adult fare. What is the limit of 12 in the code, in this chain?
notes.back: The defect (fault, bug).
notes.explanation: It is the imperfection left in the work product, present whether or not anyone is charged wrongly.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer, rushed before a public holiday, misreads the rule and sets the child-fare age limit to 12 instead of 16. A 14-year-old is then charged the adult fare. What is the overcharge, in this chain?
notes.back: The failure.
notes.explanation: It is the event during execution in which the system does not meet its requirements.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between an error and a defect?
notes.back: An error is a human action; a defect is the resulting imperfection in a work product.
notes.explanation: One is something a person does, the other something left in the product.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a defect and a failure?
notes.back: A defect is in a work product; a failure is an event during execution in which the system does not meet its requirements.
notes.explanation: A defect can sit unnoticed for years; a failure is the moment it shows, if it ever does.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between a root cause and an error?
notes.back: A root cause is the fundamental reason for a problem, such as a situation leading to an error; the error is the mistaken action.
notes.explanation: Fixing an error’s consequences handles one defect; addressing a root cause aims to stop similar ones.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When is root cause analysis typically performed?
notes.back: When a failure occurs or a defect is identified.
notes.explanation: It is triggered by a problem that has already appeared, and looks further back than the defect itself.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is believed to follow from addressing a root cause, for example by removing it?
notes.back: Similar failures or defects can be prevented, or become less frequent.
notes.explanation: The syllabus hedges this as a belief, not a guarantee.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Three releases in a row ship with broken translations. The team fixes each one, then asks why translators keep receiving the text too late. What is this last step?
notes.back: B: root cause analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Debugging
B) Root cause analysis
C) Confirmation testing
notes.choicesExplained: A removes the individual defects, which was already done. C checks that a fix worked; it does not ask why the problem keeps recurring.
notes.explanation: Asking what situation keeps producing the errors is the search for a root cause.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.2.3 “Errors, Defects, Failures, and Root Causes”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How many testing principles does the syllabus describe?
notes.back: Seven.
notes.explanation: They are general guidelines, suggested over the years, that apply to all testing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does testing show, according to the first testing principle?
notes.back: The presence of defects, not their absence.
notes.explanation: Each passing test makes it less likely that defects are still hidden, but a clean run is never proof that the test object is correct.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: After 4,000 passing tests, a manager announces that the app “has no defects”. Which principle does this claim ignore?
notes.back: A: testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects.
notes.choices:
A) Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects
B) Tests wear out
C) Absence-of-defects fallacy
notes.choicesExplained: B is about repeated tests losing their power to find new defects. C is about a verified system still failing users’ needs, not about proving no defects.
notes.explanation: Passing tests reduce the chance of undiscovered defects but cannot prove there are none.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 17
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is testing everything feasible?
notes.back: Only in trivial cases: exhaustive testing is impossible.
notes.explanation: This is the second principle; the effort has to be focused instead.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Rather than trying to test exhaustively, what should be used to focus test effort?
notes.back: Test techniques, test case prioritisation and risk-based testing.
notes.explanation: Each narrows an impossible space of tests down to the ones most worth running.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A booking form has 12 fields, each accepting hundreds of values. A tester proposes trying every combination before release. Which principle argues against the plan?
notes.back: B: exhaustive testing is impossible.
notes.choices:
A) Defects cluster together
B) Exhaustive testing is impossible
C) Testing is context dependent
notes.choicesExplained: A would steer effort towards risky areas but is not the objection to trying everything. C says approaches differ by context; it does not rule out this plan by itself.
notes.explanation: The combinations are astronomically many, so the effort has to be focused with techniques, prioritisation and risk.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why does early testing save time and money?
notes.back: A defect removed early cannot spread into the work products built from it, and fewer failures turn up later.
notes.explanation: The cost of quality falls as a result.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: To find defects early, which kinds of testing should start as early as possible?
notes.back: Both static testing and dynamic testing.
notes.explanation: Early testing is not only reviews of documents: dynamic tests should also start as soon as they can.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team reviews the user stories for a loyalty scheme before any code is written and finds that two stories contradict each other. Which principle does this illustrate?
notes.back: A: early testing saves time and money.
notes.choices:
A) Early testing saves time and money
B) Tests wear out
C) Exhaustive testing is impossible
notes.choicesExplained: B concerns repeating old tests. C concerns testing everything; neither is about when testing starts.
notes.explanation: Removing the contradiction now stops it spreading into the design, code and tests built from those stories.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the principle “defects cluster together” say?
notes.back: Most defects found, or most failures in operation, usually come from a few components.
notes.explanation: It is an illustration of the Pareto principle.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which clusters of defects are an important input for risk-based testing?
notes.back: Predicted clusters and the actual clusters observed in testing or in operation.
notes.explanation: Risk-based testing comes in chapter 5; defect clusters are one of its inputs.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In an insurance system, 3 of 40 modules account for most defects reported over two years. The test lead moves extra effort to those 3. Which principle is she using?
notes.back: A: defects cluster together.
notes.choices:
A) Defects cluster together
B) Early testing saves time and money
C) Testing shows the presence of defects
notes.choicesExplained: B is about starting testing sooner. C is about what testing can prove, not where to aim it.
notes.explanation: Observed clusters feed risk-based decisions on where to test hardest.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What happens to tests that are repeated many times?
notes.back: They find fewer and fewer new defects.
notes.explanation: This is the principle that tests wear out.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How can the wear-out effect on tests be overcome?
notes.back: By changing existing tests and their test data, and by writing new tests.
notes.explanation: Refreshing tests and their data is the syllabus’s answer to the wear-out effect.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When can repeating the same tests have a beneficial outcome?
notes.back: In some cases, for example automated regression testing.
notes.explanation: The syllabus names this as an exception to the wear-out principle.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: For two years a team has run the same 150 manual checks on its shop each release. They still all pass, yet customers keep reporting new problems. Which principle explains this?
notes.back: A: tests wear out.
notes.choices:
A) Tests wear out
B) Defects cluster together
C) Absence-of-defects fallacy
notes.choicesExplained: B concerns where defects gather. C concerns meeting users’ needs, not the dwindling power of old tests.
notes.explanation: The same tests repeated many times lose their power to find new defects; they need refreshing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the principle “testing is context dependent” say?
notes.back: No one approach suits all testing; how you test depends on the situation.
notes.explanation: What suits one product and setting may be wrong for another.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A consultant insists the insulin-pump team should test exactly as her last client, a mobile puzzle-game studio, did. Which principle warns against this?
notes.back: A: testing is context dependent.
notes.choices:
A) Testing is context dependent
B) Exhaustive testing is impossible
C) Tests wear out
notes.choicesExplained: B is about testing everything. C is about repeated tests; neither addresses copying an approach across very different products.
notes.explanation: A safety-critical medical device and a casual game call for very different testing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the absence-of-defects fallacy?
notes.back: The mistaken belief that verifying the software is enough to make the system a success.
notes.explanation: Testing all specified requirements and fixing every defect found can still produce a system that fails its users.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What might a thoroughly verified system, with every found defect fixed, still fail to do?
notes.back: Meet users’ needs and expectations, help achieve the customer’s business goals, or compare well with competitors.
notes.explanation: Verification checks against the specification; none of these is guaranteed by it.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the absence-of-defects fallacy, what should be carried out in addition to verification?
notes.back: Validation.
notes.explanation: Validation checks the system against users’ and stakeholders’ needs, which verification alone does not.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council’s parking app passed every specified test and has no known defects, but residents find it slower than the old paper permits and keep using the paper. Which principle does this show?
notes.back: A: the absence-of-defects fallacy.
notes.choices:
A) Absence-of-defects fallacy
B) Testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects
C) Defects cluster together
notes.choicesExplained: B is about testing being unable to prove there are no defects; the problem here is not a hidden defect. C is about where defects concentrate.
notes.explanation: A verified, defect-free system can still fail users’ needs; validation was missing.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the first principle differ from the seventh (absence-of-defects fallacy)?
notes.back: The first: testing cannot prove there are no defects. The seventh: even a verified system may not meet users’ needs.
notes.explanation: One is about the limits of what testing can prove; the other is about verification without validation.
notes.contrast: Principle 1: the limit of proof. Principle 7: right product versus product built right.
notes.source: CTFL Syllabus v4.0.1, 1.3 “Testing Principles”, p. 18
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
